passages.text: Epitope and Paratope Mapping of a SUMO-Remnant Antibody Using Cross-Linking Mass Spectrometry and Molecular Docking

The small ubiquitin-like modifier (SUMO) is an important post-translational modification that regulates the function of various proteins essential for DNA damage repair, genome integrity, and cell homeostasis. To identify protein SUMOylation effectively, an enrichment step is necessary, often requiring exogenous gene expression in cells and immunoaffinity purification of SUMO-remnant peptides following tryptic digestion. Previously, an antibody was developed to enrich tryptic peptides containing the remnant NQTGG on the receptor lysine, although the specifics of the structural interaction motif remained unclear. This study integrates de novo sequencing, intact mass spectrometry, cross-linking mass spectrometry, and molecular docking to elucidate the structural interaction motifs of a SUMO-remnant antibody. Additional cross-linking experiments were performed using SUMOylated peptides and high-field asymmetric waveform ion mobility spectrometry (FAIMS) to enhance the sensitivity and confirm interactions at the paratope interface. This study establishes a robust framework for characterizing antibody–antigen interactions, offering valuable insights into the structural basis of SUMO-remnant peptide recognition.
Introduction

SUMOylation is a reversible post-translational modification that forms an isopeptide bond between small ubiquitin-related modifier (SUMO) and lysine side chains of protein substrates. This modification can enhance or inhibit protein interactions, stability, and localization, critically regulating processes like DNA damage repair, transcription, and signal transduction.− Identifying endogenous SUMOylation sites by mass spectrometry (MS) is challenging due to the dynamic nature of SUMOylation and the complex MS/MS spectra from the branched SUMO remnants of tryptic peptides. We previously developed a 6xHis-SUMO3-Q87R/Q88N mutant that facilitates the identification of SUMOylated peptides by MS. We also produced a monoclonal antibody that enriches peptides containing the SUMO remnant (NQTGG) left after trypsin digestion. Similar approaches, such as the SUMO3 T90K mutant or the SUMO2 T91R mutant, utilize commercially available anti-diglycine antibodies for identifying SUMO sites.

The high specificity of this antibody toward its target antigen allowed for the enrichment of SUMO peptides, providing a useful tool for in vitro SUMOylation assays, identification of SUMO E3 ligase substrates, and crosstalk with other ubiquitin-like modifiers. However, the specific interactions between the epitope (SUMO remnant) and the complementary amino acids of the antibody (paratope) remain unclear. The interactions at the paratope–epitope interface depend on the specific binding between the NQTGG tag and the three hypervariable regions known as complementarity-determining regions (CDRs) present in both the variable domains of the heavy and light chains of the SUMO-remnant antibody. Determining the residues involved in paratope–epitope interactions is essential for enhancing antibody specificity, affinity, and stability, which are critical for improving the efficiency and purity of immunoaffinity purification.

Currently, various approaches are available for investigating antigen-binding sites. Traditional structural biology methods such as nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) and X-ray crystallography face limitations due to the size of the complex and the significant labor required, restricting their widespread use.− Advances in predictive tools have shown good alignment with experimental data but have been unsuccessful in modeling antibody–antigen complexes. Consequently, mass spectrometry-based strategies have emerged as superior alternatives due to their enhanced sensitivity and simplicity compared to traditional structure-based techniques. Covalent labeling (CL-MS), hydrogen–deuterium exchange (HDX), and chemical cross-linking− (CX-MS) coupled with MS have been used, either as stand-alone techniques or in combination, to probe epitope and paratope interactions.

One limitation of HDX experiments is the need for labor-intensive procedures and reliance on specialized laboratory equipment. Additional drawbacks include enzyme restrictions and challenges in distinguishing between direct binding and conformational changes after complex formation. While CL-MS does not suffer from the same limitations, it also exhibits issues related to indirect binding interactions that could lead to false epitope/paratope identification. On the other hand, CX-MS provides complementary and additional information to HDX data, aligns with crystallography data, and has been shown to enhance the prediction of antibody–antigen complexes. Although CX-MS exhibits certain limitations due to a limited number of reactive residues, steric hindrance upon binding, and the intricate nature of cross-linked reaction mixtures, ongoing progress in MS and the emergence of novel cross-linkers offer potential solutions to these issues. However, the fact that the antibody paratope amino sequence is usually not known limits its application to indirect measurements, as previously performed where changes in partially hydrolyzed disuccinimidyl suberate (DSS) in the presence and absence of the antibody provided information on the epitope. To better understand the recognition mechanism, the antibody sequence is required.

De novo protein sequencing by mass spectrometry is very useful to confirm sequence identity and protein modifications when no cDNA or hybridoma cell line is available and has nearly fully replaced Edman degradation. Moreover, it has been used in an automated fashion to assemble different antibodies. In a standard de novo antibody sequencing experiment, multiple enzymes are employed, and the identified peptides from a typical bottom-up approach are assembled.

Here, we adapted a previously validated protocol to sequence the monoclonal antibody against the SUMO mutant remnant and then probed the interactions between the epitope and the paratope using chemical cross-linking. We performed several cross-linking experiments, providing information about the paratope peptides directly involved in binding the SUMO-remnant chain, which correlated well with the predicted structure.
Materials and Methods
De Novo Sequencing of SUMO-Remnant Antibody

The sample preparation protocol was an adaptation of Peng et al. with a few modifications. Briefly, the SUMO-remnant antibody (UMO-1–7–7, available upon request to Abcam) was denatured in 2% sodium deoxycholate (SDC), 200 mM Tris-HCl, and 10 mM Tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine (TCEP, Thermo Fisher Scientific), pH 8.0, at 95 °C for 10 min, followed by 30 min incubation at 37 °C. The sample was then alkylated with 20 mM 2-chloroacetamide (Aldrich). For selected proteolytic digestion, 3 μg of antibody was digested by one of the following proteases: trypsin (Promega), chymotrypsin (Promega), lys-C (Wako), glu-C (Promega), asp-N (Promega), thermolysin (Promega), and elastase (Promega) in a 1:50 ratio (w/w) in a total volume of 100 μL of 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate at 37 °C for 16 h. For sequential digestion, the antibody was first digested with trypsin for 16 h, followed by the addition of chymotrypsin and incubation for 4 h at 37 °C. For digestion with pepsin (Promega), 3 μg of antibody was digested at 37 °C and pH 2.0 for 16 h. After digestion, SDC was removed by adding 2 μL of formic acid (FA), and the sample was centrifuged at 14,000g for 20 min. The supernatant containing proteolytic peptides was collected and desalted using Ultra Micro Spin columns (The Nest Group) according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

Vacuum-dried peptides were resuspended in 4% FA and analyzed by liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry/MS (LC-MS/MS) using an Easy nLC1000 coupled to an Orbitrap Fusion Tribrid mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Peptide separation was performed on a custom C18 column (Jupiter, Phenomenex, 3 μm, 300 Å, 150 μm × 30 cm) with a flow rate of 600 nL/min and a linear gradient of 5–38% acetonitrile (ACN,0.2% FA) in 105 min, followed by 3 min at 90% ACN (0.2%FA) and 12 min re-equilibration at 5% ACN (0.2% FA). Full MS scans were acquired at a resolution of 60,000 at m/z 200, with a target AGC of 5E5 and a maximum injection time of 120 ms. MS/MS scans were acquired in HCD mode with a stepped collision energy of 25, 35, and 50 at a resolution of 30,000 using a loop count of 20, a target AGC 2E3, and a maximum injection time of 250 ms. The MS/MS triggering threshold was set at 8E3, and the dynamic exclusion of the previously acquired precursor was enabled for 30 s. All raw files were searched with the PEAKS AB engine (Bioinformatics Solutions, Inc., Version 2.0). Parent and fragment mass tolerances were 12 ppm and 0.02 Da, respectively. A maximum of 8 variable modifications were allowed per peptide, including oxidation (MHW), deamidation (NQ), carbamidomethylation (C), and Pyro-glu from Q.
Intact Mass Analysis

The SUMO-remnant antibody was digested with IdeS (FabRICATOR, Genovis), deglycosylated with PNGase F (Thermo Fisher Scientific), and reduced with 5 mM TCEP prior to MS analysis. Intact mass analysis was performed on a Q-Exactive HF BioPharma platform (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Proteins were loaded on a C4 precolumn (Optimize Technologies) and separated on a custom C8 column (Aeris C8, Phenomenex, 3.6 μm, 200 Å, 150 μm × 25 cm) connected to a Nanoflex electrospray source. Proteins were loaded on a C4 precolumn (Optimize Technologies) and eluted at 600 nL/min with a linear gradient of 5–80% solvent B (80% ACN, 0.2% FA) in 40 min and held at 100% B for 5 min. Full MS scans were obtained at a resolution of 240,000, with 3 microscans and a maximum IT of 200 ms with an AGC target of 1e6. Deconvolution was conducted using Thermo Biopharma Finder software version 5.1 with the Xtract algorithm.
SUMOylation Assay

In vitro SUMOylation was performed as previously described. Briefly, recombinant 6xHis-SUMO3-Q87R/Q88N was incubated at 37 °C with the SAE1/SAE2 heterodimer protein, UBC9, and 1 μL of 100 mM MgATP. The sample was reduced with 5 mM TCEP and alkylated with 10 mM 2-chloroacetamide. Digestion was performed overnight with trypsin at a 1:50 enzyme-to-peptide ratio. Peptides were desalted using an Ultra Micro Spin column.
Immunopurification of SUMO Peptides and Cross-Linking Mass Spectrometry

Desalted peptides or synthetic peptides containing the NQTGG side chain were incubated overnight at 4 °C with the SUMO-remnant antibody in PBS or immobilized on MagReSyn Protein A magnetic beads. The peptides/antibodies were then cross-linked with either DSS, DSSO, or TBDSPP (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at a final concentration of 2 mM. The cross-linking reaction was carried out for 1 h at room temperature and quenched with 500 mM NH4HCO3 to obtain a final concentration of 20 mM. Samples were then transferred on a 3 K molecular cut-off (VWR), washed twice with 200 μL of 50 mM NH4HCO3, and centrifuged at 13,000g for 10 min. Samples were reconstituted in 190 μL of 50 mM NH4HCO3 reduced with 5 mM TCEP and alkylated with 10 mM 2-chloroacetamide. Digestion was performed overnight with chymotrypsin at a 1:20 enzyme-to-peptide ratio. Peptides were desalted using Ultra Micro Spin columns. TBDSPP-cross-linked peptides were enriched with a Titansphere Phos-TiO kit (GL Science, Tokyo, Japan).

LC-MS/MS analyses of cross-linked peptides were performed on an Orbitrap Exploris 480. Peptides were loaded on a C4 precolumn (Optimize Technologies) and separated on a C18 column (Jupiter, Phenomenex, 3 μm, 300 Å, 150 μm × 30 cm) with a flow rate of 600 nL/min and a linear gradient of 10–100% solvent B (80% ACN, 0.2% FA) in 100 min and held at 100% B for 2 min. Full MS scans were obtained from m/z 350 to 1100 at a resolution of 240,000, a maximum IT of 50 ms, with a normalized AGC target of 100%. MS/MS spectra of precursor ions with charge states 2–8 were acquired for a maximum of 3 s at a resolution of 45,000, intensity threshold 4000, normalized AGC target at 50%, and a maximum injection time at 1000 ms. The isolation window was set to 1.2 Th with a 34% HCD normalized collision energy (NCE). A dynamic exclusion time of 30 s was used for all of the MS/MS acquisitions. For samples cross-linked with TBDSPP, analyses were also performed on an Orbitrap Exploris 480 using a FAIMS Pro device (Thermo Fisher Scientific) operating at standard resolution mode (inner and outer electrodes maintained at 100 °C) with nitrogen as a carrier gas flowing at 4 L/min. 3-CV combinations (−40/–55/–70) were selected. For samples cross-linked with DSSO, raw files were searched with MaxLynx integrated into the MaxQuant environment with the suggested parameters in the step-by-step guideline with few modifications. Briefly, the second specificity of DSSO was modified as KSTY, and digestion was set as specific with chymotrypsin and 3 missed cleavages. The minimum peptide length was set at 5, and the maximum peptide mass as 10,000 Da. Finally, a PSM FDR cross-link of 5% was used. For sample cross-linked with TBDSPP, data were analyzed using the XlinkX node of Proteome Discoverer 2.3 and the XlinkX_Cleavable processing and consensus workflows, selecting cross-links with a False Discovery Rate of 5%. Finally, cross-linked samples with DSS were searched with pLink 2. Custom parameters were used as follows: nonspecific digestion with up to 5 missed cleavages, 20 ppm for precursor and fragment tolerance, fixed carbamidomethylation [C], variable oxidation [M], and deamidation [NQ] with 5% FDR.
EThcD

EThcD analysis was performed on an Orbitrap Ascend with an Evosep One system. Peptides were loaded onto individual Evosep for desalting, washed with 20 μL of 0.1% FA, and then separated with a 15 cm × 75 μm IonOpticks Aurora Series UHPLC column and a Whisper Zoom 20 SPD gradient. Full MS scans were obtained from m/z 400 to 800 at a resolution of 120,000, a maximum IT of 50 ms, with a normalized AGC target of 100%. DDA MS/MS spectra of precursor ions with charge states 2–6 were acquired for a maximum of 3 s at a resolution of 60,000, a scan range of 140–2000 m/z, normal AGC target at 1000%, isolation window set to 1 Th, ETD reaction time of 123 ms, and HCD supplemental activation collisional energy set at 60%. A dynamic exclusion time of 60 s was used for all MS/MS acquisitions.
Targeted LC-MS/MS Analyses Using Parallel Reaction Monitoring

Parallel reaction monitoring (PRM) was performed on a Q-Exactive HF BioPharma platform with an Easy-nLC 1200. Peptides were loaded on a C4 precolumn (Optimize Technologies) and separated on a homemade C18 column (JupiterC18, Phenomenex, 3 μm, 300 Å, 150 μm × 30 cm) with a flow rate of 600 nL/min and a linear gradient of 6–45% solvent B (80% ACN, 0.2% FA) in 105 min and held at 90% B for 3 min. HCD at 27% with a 1.4 Th isolation window was used for the PRM experiment. MS/MS resolution, automatic gain control, and injection time were set at 60 K, 5E4, and 150 ms, respectively. The MS raw data have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium () via the PRIDE partner repository with the data set identifier PXD055077, PXD055085 and PXD060724.
Structure Prediction and Molecular Docking

The structure of the light chain and the SUMO-remnant peptide was predicted using the ESMFold algorithm, while the heavy chain was predicted using the ColabFold algorithm as implemented on the Colab server. DisVis webserveur− was used to evaluate the information content of MS cross-links and identify possible false positives. The SUMO peptide was then docked using HADDOCK 2.4 using the cross-link distance restraints. The results of the molecular docking were visualized using PyMOL (1.1r1).
Glycan Search

A glycopeptide database search was performed on all raw files from de novo sequencing using the glycan search workflow in PEAKS studio 11 against the constructed sequence of the SUMO-remnant antibody. The search parameters were set as follows: up to 3 missed cleavages, 20 ppm precursor mass tolerance, and 0.02 Da fragment mass tolerance; carbamidomethylation (C), deamidation (NQ), oxidation (M), and pyro-glu form Q were set as variable modifications. NH4 adduct was considered with a maximum of one adduct per peptide and a maximum of 2 fucoses.
Result and Discussion
De Novo Sequencing of SUMO-Remnant Antibody

To identify the paratope of anti-K-NQTGG, we first conducted de novo sequencing and peptide assembly using Peaks Ab software (Figure 1, top panel). Our protocol was adapted from Peng et al. with a few modifications. Specifically, we either used eight proteases with complementary specificities or combined chymotrypsin with trypsin in sequential digestion (Supporting Figures 1 and 2).

Previous studies have shown that consecutive proteolytic digestion increases the number of identified proteins, whereas sequential digestion with trypsin and elastase allows for the identification of cross-links in inaccessible regions, as exemplified for the TAF4–12 complex. Conversely, sequential digestion of SUMO-remnant antibody with trypsin and chymotrypsin resulted in fewer peptides (Figures S1 and S2) but provided more fragment ions covering the N-terminus of the light chain, leading to a higher confidence score (indicated by the plot line in Figure S1).

Before digestion, the antibody was denatured with sodium deoxycholate at a high temperature in the presence of TCEP. This resulted in nearly complete desulfurization of all cysteine residues in the constructed sequence. Although this conversion has been demonstrated before at lower levels, it should be considered during peptide assembly to avoid incorrect assignment. To mitigate this potential issue, it is advisable to use another reducing reagent, such as DTT, as previously mentioned. In the case of the SUMO-remnant antibody, all cysteine residues in the constructed light and heavy chains were assigned as alanine, except for the one at the C-terminus of the light chain. Under harsher conditions, converting cysteine to alanine yielded more favorable results, considering the desulfurization process. Without denatured conditions, the constructed sequences had more errors, particularly in the third CDR of the light chain, which was poorly covered (results not shown).

Using the adapted protocol, we achieved 100% coverage on both light and heavy chains with a score of 99.2% (Supporting Figure 3). Excluding cysteine desulfurization, only two amino acids on the heavy chain needed further confirmation. On the heavy chain, asparagine residues 166 and 378 were incorrectly identified as aspartic acid due to deamidation, which can occur during manufacturing, storage, or sample preparation. Our protein modification profiles revealed a high occurrence of deamidation in tryptic digest (high pH) and a low occurrence in pepsin digest (low pH), consistent with published data on endopeptidase Glu-C at low pH. To differentiate between the isomeric residues leucine and isoleucine, Peaks Ab employed a basic local alignment search tool (BLAST) using the constructed sequence. Additionally, it calculates the number of peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs) from chymotrypsin and pepsin digests, where Ile or Leu residues occur at the C-terminus. These enzymes preferentially cleave at the C-terminus of leucine over isoleucine, aiding in residue-specific assignment. To further improve the confidence in Ile/Leu differentiation, we applied an EThcD approach to both tryptic and chymotryptic digests. Briefly, z-ions were generated through electron-transfer dissociation (ETD) fragmentation of doubly or triply charged peptide precursor ions. These z-ions were subsequently fragmented using higher-energy collisional dissociation (HCD) with broadband ion isolation, producing w-ions that provided diagnostic fragment ions for the differentiation of leucine and isoleucine residues. This approach effectively leveraged the diagnostic w- and z-ions to support accurate residue identification, with results confirmed independently through cDNA sequencing. Representative examples, including tryptic peptides from the complementarity-determining regions (CDRs) of the light and heavy chains, are provided in Supporting Figure 4. Following de novo sequencing of the SUMO-remnant antibody, we next performed a structure prediction for both the light and heavy chains using the AlphaFold and ESMFold.

A glycan analysis revealed that asparagine 291 (highlighted in purple in Supporting Figure 5) on the heavy chain is modified with over 50 different N-linked glycans with a significant presence of highly fucosylated glycans. Supporting Figure 6 presents a pie chart displaying the distribution of these glycans. The three most prominent glycopeptide spectra, along with their corresponding compositions and highlighted fragments, are shown in Supporting Figure 7. Altogether, the combination of a limited set of enzymes (trypsin, chymotrypsin, asp-N, and trypsin + chymotrypsin) provided good coverage of both the light and heavy chains, validated the sequence predicted from the hybridoma cDNA, and identified N-linked glycans that could not be inferred from cDNA sequencing.
Sequence Validation by Intact Mass Measurements

Next, we verified the assembled sequence through intact mass analysis (Figure 1, second panel). Briefly, the subunits of the SUMO-remnant antibody were obtained by deglycosylation with PNGase F, digestion with IdeS (FabRICATOR), and reduction with TCEP. Using FabRICATOR (IdeS) allowed us to apply identical resolution settings for both the light and heavy chains, resulting in isotopically resolved spectra. This protease cleaves the antibody just below the hinge, precisely at a single amino acid position (Figure 1, second panel). Upon reduction, it produces the Fc/2 and Fd′ fragments, both of which exhibit a mass similar to that of the light chain. We confirmed one deamidation of the heavy chain in the Fc2 fragment (Figure 2).

Additionally, we validated the expected conversion of the N-terminal glutamine to pyro-glutamic acid, resulting in a mass difference of 17 Da in both the light and heavy sequences. Accordingly, we observed a 6 Da mass shift for the light chain and 4 Da for both fragments of the heavy chain (Figure 2 and Supporting Figure 8). We hypothesize that the observed mass difference could be explained by the conservation of intrachain disulfide bonds, which are more solvent-exposed, contrasting with the interchain disulfide bonds. We validated this hypothesis by performing intact mass analyses with and without alkylation. The mass difference between the two monoisotopic masses highlights the cysteine modification and the number of expected S–S bonds. Theoretically, for the reduced/alkylated light chain, we should observe a mass increase of 399 Da corresponding to seven carbamidomethylated cysteines. However, we identified a mass difference of 57 Da, which can be attributed solely to only one carbamidomethylated cysteine, as shown in Supporting Figure 9.

Moreover, with the constructed sequence for the Fc/2 fragment, we observed an approximate mass shift of 30 Da. This mass difference could be explained by the substitution of alanine 303 to threonine, confirmed by MS/MS with a high-confidence score and validated by intact mass measurements (Supporting Figure 8). This permutation appears to be lot-dependent and does not affect the isolation of the SUMO-remnant antibody (data not shown). Altogether, intact mass measurements from the antibody fragment chains enabled the correlation of the sequence information available from the multienzyme digestion experiments. For convenience, the amino acid sequence of the light and heavy chains of the SUMO-remnant antibody is shown in Supporting Figure 5.
Paratope Mapping by Cross-Linking Mass Spectrometry and Molecular Docking

Following de novo sequencing and validation of the antibody sequence through intact mass measurements, we investigated the interaction occurring at the paratope–epitope interface using cross-linking mass spectrometry (Figure 1, panel 2 bottom panel). Prior to cross-linking with DSS, the SUMO-remnant antibody was incubated with peptide K*NQTGG, where * indicates the isopeptide bound between the epsilon NH2 of Lys and the C-terminus of Gly. To achieve optimal coverage, we employed the same protocol used for de novo sequencing, excluding Lys-C, and used sodium deoxycholate as a denaturing agent. The raw data were analyzed using pLink with nonspecific digestion parameters. Applying a 5% false discovery rate (FDR), we identified 19 cross-linked peptides, including four mapped within the CDR as confirmed by IMGT/DomainGapAlign and ProABC-2 predictions. We next evaluated distance restraints between the SUMO-remnant antibody and the K*NQTGG peptide using the DisVis web server (Supporting Table S1). Each restraint was assigned a Z-score to estimate the likelihood of false positives. DisVis identified solutions consistent with up to 11 restraints, indicating the potential presence of up to eight false positives. To model the interactions between the antibody and the SUMO-remnant pentapeptide, we utilized HADDOCK. Filtered cross-links were incorporated as unambiguous distance restraints, supplemented by center-of-mass restraints, to generate a refined structural model. The top-ranked cluster is shown in Supporting Figure 10. This initial model places the pentapeptide near the C-terminal region of the heavy chain without forming direct interactions with the predicted CDRs. To evaluate the validity of the docking model, we re-examined the filtered restraints excluded during docking and identified them as potential false positives by DisVis. Specifically, we focused on four cross-links mapped to residues within the CDRs. Given the high false discovery rate associated with cross-linking of serine, threonine, and tyrosine residues, we performed validation using parallel reaction monitoring (PRM) analysis on a Q-Exactive mass spectrometer (Supporting Figure 11). This analysis confirmed the precise assignment of all four cross-linked peptides, each located within the 30 Å threshold and proximal to the CDRs, effectively invalidating the initial model. We hypothesize that over-cross-linking may have introduced nonspecific interactions, misinterpreted as true structural information. Consequently, we refined the docking restraints based on the updated DisVis analysis (Figure 3). In the revised model, the pentapeptide occupies a gap between the light and heavy chains, positioned closer to the CDRs, aligning with the validated cross-linking data. This improved model provides a more accurate depiction of the interaction between the antibody and the SUMO-remnant pentapeptide.

To further investigate the specificity of the SUMO-remnant antibody and our model, we incubated a pool of synthetic peptides at 50 nM from 40 known SUMO substrates, all containing the NQTGG side chain lysine. Cross-linking was performed in solution using DSS and the raw files were analyzed using MaxLynx integrated into the MaxQuant environment. Chymotrypsin was selected as the proteolytic enzyme due to its comprehensive coverage across both light and heavy chains, whereas trypsin yields fewer peptides near the third CDR of the light chain (Supporting Figures 1 and 2). To address the challenge of the expansion of the computational search space exacerbated by the SUMO remnant, lysine-containing side chain NQTGG was introduced as a linear segment into the peptide FASTA sequence. One drawback of this modification is the reduced sequence database search score due to the number of unidentified fragment ions. Consequently, we opted for a higher FDR and manually validated the MS/MS, specifically scrutinizing the diagnostic SUMO peaks. Using this approach, we identified nine cross-linked peptides containing the NQTGG motif. Among these, one overlapped with previous experiments on peptide K*NQTGG (Supporting Figure 11), six were located within the CDR of the light chain, and three were within the constant region of the heavy chain of the antibody (Supporting Table S2), but identified as potential positive restraint. Furthermore, we conducted additional cross-linking experiments using the peptide FKQEPEPEDELPEAPK, modified with either the SUMO-remnant NQTGG or its reverse sequence, GGTQN (Supporting Figure 12). These experiments confirmed that the SUMO-remnant antibody selectively binds to the NQTGG epitope, while its reverse sequence, GGTQN, is not recognized by the antibody, underscoring the epitope’s orientation specificity.

To minimize nonspecific cross-linking and false positives, we next incubated peptide FK*QEPEPEDELPEAPK (*designates modified lysine residues) with the SUMO-remnant antibody previously cross-linked on MagReSyn Protein A magnetic beads. We performed two washes to remove weak and nonspecific interactions prior to cross-linking with DSSO. As in the previous analysis, chymotrypsin was used. Interestingly, our observations revealed only cross-linked peptides containing the NQTGG motif between the first and second CDR of the light chain, which are in close proximity. An example is shown in Figure 4 for the cross-linked peptide YQHRPGQPPKQLIY. Notably, we observed the presence of fragment ions from the SUMO-remnant chain (highlighted in yellow).

Finally, we performed a cross-linking experiment with a poly SUMO chain protein obtained from in vitro SUMOylation of SUMO3m (Supporting Figure 13), which contains a lysine at position 22. To address sensitivity issues related to the low abundance of the cross-linked peptides, we used TBDSPP for enrichment and gas-phase separation using high-field asymmetric waveform ion mobility spectrometry (FAIMS). This additional separation and enrichment enabled the identification of the tryptic peptide EGVKTENDHINLK derived from SUMO3m, featuring SUMOylated K22 cross-linked with the chymotryptic peptide SLSRY from the heavy chain of the antibody, associated with the first CDR (Supporting Figure 14). These findings align with our previous observations and emphasize the critical interactions at the paratope. Additionally, the results corroborate the predictions illustrated in Figure 5, which were generated using validated restraints (light-K30, light-K46, light-S57, heavy-S27, heavy-Y31, and heavy-Y98), as detailed in Figure 4, and Supporting Figures 9 and 12, with an upper distance limit of 30 Å. The top three HADDOCK models suggest that the NQTGG motif is positioned within a groove formed by the interplay of various complementarity-determining regions (CDRs). This motif establishes multiple contacts with residues in the third CDR of the heavy chain, a region centrally located within the antigen-binding site of both the heavy and light chains. Notably, consistent polar interactions were observed between tyrosine 98, arginine 104, and, to a lesser extent, arginine 95 and serine 99 on the H3 loop, strongly indicating that these residues play a pivotal role in antigen binding.

While we acknowledge the limitations inherent in using cross-linking data and molecular docking to predict antibody–antigen complexes, as highlighted in previous studies, these challenges are further compounded by the absence of models that explicitly account for the branched structure of the SUMO peptide. Nonetheless, our findings are consistent with prior studies that underscore the importance of tyrosine residues in antigen–antibody interactions and highlight the significance of the third CDR in antigen binding. Ultimately, the precise identification of critical residues for binding would require additional experiments, such as the systematic substitution of amino acid residues (alanine scanning), to assess their impact on binding affinity.
Conclusions

In this study, we employed an innovative approach to elucidate the structural interaction motifs of the SUMO-remnant antibody, aiming to enhance our understanding of the paratope–epitope interaction. Gaining deeper insights into the interaction motifs that govern the selective binding of the SUMO remnant is essential for the rational design and engineering of more effective antibodies and nanobodies. The integration of de novo sequencing, intact mass measurements, cross-linking mass spectrometry, and molecular docking enabled the identification of the interacting regions within the antibody’s CDR and the SUMO-remnant epitope. The combination of multiple proteases with complementary specificities significantly improved the identification of proteins and cross-links, particularly in regions previously considered inaccessible. Our protocol modifications provided a higher confidence score for peptide assembly, especially for the N-terminus of the light chain.

The use of sodium deoxycholate for denaturation and TCEP for reduction resulted in near-complete desulfurization of cysteine residues, enabling accurate peptide assignment and minimizing incorrect residue identification. Sequence validation through intact mass measurements confirmed the cDNA sequence from the hybridoma, identifying minimal errors and validating the presence of modifications such as deamidation and N-terminal glutamine conversion to pyro-glutamic acid.

Cross-linking mass spectrometry further delineated the paratope–epitope interactions, revealing key cross-linked peptides within the CDRs. The use of DSS for cross-linking and subsequent validation through parallel reaction monitoring (PRM) and MaxLynx software underscored the specificity and accuracy of our findings. The use of FAIMS for peptide separation and enrichment marked a significant improvement in detecting low-abundance cross-linked peptides, providing detailed insights into the antibody–antigen interaction.

A critical component of our workflow was the incorporation of electron transfer/higher-energy collision dissociation (EThcD), which enabled differentiation between isomeric residues such as leucine and isoleucine. By leveraging diagnostic fragment ions (z- and w-ions), EThcD provided a higher confidence level in residue identification, particularly within challenging CDR regions. This approach not only confirmed assignments derived from de novo sequencing but also improved the accuracy of peptide assembly, highlighting its importance in high-resolution mass spectrometry workflows for antibody characterization.

Achieving 100% sequence coverage for both the light and the heavy chains of the antibody allowed for the precise identification of CDR residues involved in paratope interactions. Specifically, the consistent polar contact observed on the H3 loop of the heavy chain, particularly involving tyrosine 98, arginine 104, arginine 95, and serine 99, underscored the structural dynamics and critical determinants of antibody–antigen binding. These insights lay a foundation for improving the affinity and selectivity of SUMO-remnant antibodies. Overall, our comprehensive analyses not only elucidate the interaction motif of the SUMO-remnant antibody but also establish a robust framework for future studies on SUMOylation. The use of SUMO-remnant affinity purification for protein SUMOylation profiling offers a valuable approach for large-scale analysis under diverse cellular conditions. Understanding the antibody regions that interact with the SUMO pentapeptide opens avenues for the development of single-chain antibodies or nanobodies with enhanced binding affinity and specificity, enabling more comprehensive SUMO proteomic studies.
